title: buying-inference-decision-pathways-and-pov
content:
Purpose
Short working POV to align messaging and objection handling for buying decisions where customers are evaluating managed Redwood vs running vLLM / TGI / TensorRT-LLM stacks themselves. Focus is operator burden, risk transfer, TCO signals, and the decision pathway a buyer follows from experimentation to production.

TL;DR
- Many teams choose self-hosted for perceived cost savings and control during early exploration.
- The true decision hinge between self-hosted and managed is operator uncertainty: predictable latency, burst capacity, and programmatic fallback under SLOs.
- Messaging that wins: emphasize predictable unit economics, operational SLAs, and fallbacks that preserve customer UX during infrastructure failures.

Target buyer personas (ordered by buying impact)
- ML Platform / Infrastructure Lead (Primary): cares about ownership, tooling compatibility (K8s, existing infra), and long-term maintenance cost.
- Product Engineering Manager (Feature owner): cares about latency, stability for users, rollout safety.
- CTO / Head of ML (Strategic): cares about control, vendor lock-in, regulatory exposure, and cost predictability at scale.
- DevOps / SRE (Influencer): cares about observability, tracing, alerting, error budgets and incident playbooks.

Key decision pathway (common observed pattern)
1) Exploration: PoC with open-sourced runtime (vLLM / TGI) on a single GPU, quick experiments, optimistic perf.
2) Scale anxiety: as QPS or sequence length grows, KV-cache, batching, instability appear. Cost math diverges.
3) Ops discovery: need for autoscaling, node pools, OOM handling, GPU eviction, kernel tuning. Time sinks appear.
4) SLA moment: a user-facing incident or a regulatory ask forces re-evaluation.
5) Buy vs Build: teams that buy pick Redwood when predictable latency + fallbacks + cost modeling beats incremental ops hiring.

How self-hosted tech differences play into the buyer journey
- vLLM: fast to iterate; great for single-machine experiments. Pain points: multi-GPU KV cache consistency, batching inefficiencies at real QPS, and little guidance on cost under variance. Messaging angle: "Accelerate prototyping — then let us shoulder production complexity."
- TGI (Transformer-Generic-Inference): focused on flexibility and supporting many backends. Pain points: operator plumbing, less opinionated autoscaling, and connector maintenance. Messaging: "We'll integrate with your TGI investments and take over operational runbooks."
- TensorRT-LLM / Triton-like autotuned setups: high peak efficiency but heavy infra engineering and brittle tuning per model/hardware. Pain: versioned kernel regressions, performance cliffs when sequence lengths change. Messaging: "Keep the cost advantages where they exist — but avoid the fragile edge cases that cause downtime."

Top objections and proposed responses
- "We can do it cheaper ourselves." -> Response: show end-to-end unit economics (tokens served, ops headcount, incident cost). Provide a conservative runbook amortized cost model vs Redwood committed pricing + burst. Offer a short-term audit: 2-week cluster telemetry review to estimate true run costs.
- "We need full control / on-prem / air gap." -> Response: Redwood Private + VPC option, hybrid control plane, KMS/HSM integrations. Offer architecture diagram and week-long security workshop.
- "Open-source gives us flexibility; vendor lock-in risk." -> Response: Redwood supports model portability and version pinning. Provide model export/import checklist and rollback guarantees. Emphasize standardized API contract — swap verdicts without app changes.
- "We have unique hardware (custom GPUs / NPU) or need extreme latency." -> Response: Redwood can deploy to Dedicated with custom hardware support and kernel-selection tuning; also describe our smart routing & local-region fallbacks to reduce tail latency.

Messaging frameworks and one-liners for different stages
- Exploration stage (developer-focused): "Prototype on vLLM — ship to users on Redwood in minutes when you need reliability."
- Convincing engineering managers: "Remove the 80% of infra toil that doesn't add product value — predictable latency and measurable token cost."
- Exec/Procurement: "Shift capital cost and hiring risk into predictable usage and reserved capacity contracts with SLAs."

Proof points and data to assemble (recommended quick experiments for GTM kit)
- Before/after: PoC cluster telemetry showing ops hours spent on tuning per model (claim: 40–120 person-hours per model to reach production-grade).
- Cost delta: Sample three workload types (short chat, long context summarization, embedding heavy) comparing self-hosted estimated $/million tokens vs Redwood pricing + reserved amortization.
- Reliability: Case study of canary fallback reducing user-facing errors during a GPU OOM event (anonymized).

Collateral and playbook actions for SDR/AE/RSE
- One-page "Decision Pathways" cheat sheet (deliverable).
- Two recommended audit offers: 1) 2-week runtime telemetry analysis (free for qualified accounts). 2) Cost-of-ownership workshop (paid prep, discounted if they sign).
- Technical Appendix: mapping matrix of common OSS components -> Redwood parity/advantages (vLLM: prototyping, TGI: integration, TensorRT-LLM: peak perf but brittle).

Unresolved / research items (notes to self)
- Need internal telemetry to quantify average ops-hours per model by model size and sequence length. (Ask applied-ml infra team for dataset: TELEMETRY-OPS-2024)
- Get anonymized customer examples of when a managed fallback saved an app (eng-runbooks).
- Pricing sensitivity matrix: thresholds where reserved capacity deals start to beat DIY.

Sales-ready rebuttal snippets (copyable)
- "If your team already runs vLLM at low QPS and you're happy, keep doing that for experimentation. But for predictable UX at scale, teams move to Redwood to avoid high-impact incidents and ops hiring cycles."
- "We aren't against OSS — we use it. Our value is removing the fragility: consistent SLOs, controlled rollouts, and cost visibility so you can focus product-forward."

Appendix: Example short runbook comparison (sketch)
- DIY runbook tasks: kernel tuning, KV cache sharding, manual autoscaler thresholds, preemptible GPU eviction handling, model quantization regression tests, nightly perf tests.
- Redwood runbook tasks: model onboarding checklist, model-profiled autoscaling policy, SLA incident coordination, per-route cost telemetry, one-click rollback.

Quick win experiments for next 30 days (GTM ops)
- Create a single benchmark page comparing latency/cost for a 13B LLM across: vLLM single-node, vLLM multi-node, Redwood Hosted (same model profile).
- Package a "2-week telemetry audit" offer and script for SDR outreach.

Notes to self / conversational fragments (keep)
- Keep messaging honest about where DIY wins: absolute peak perf on narrow hardware configs. Don't overclaim managed superiority on best-case synthetic perf.
- Emphasize time-to-resolve and mean-time-to-recovery as the narrative pivot rather than raw per-token microbenchmarks.

End of doc.
